The box is carried along by **friction**, and the greatest acceleration friction can
supply is **µg**.
**Step 1 — see what accelerates the box.** Nothing touches it but the floor, so the
only horizontal force available is **static friction** ✓
**Step 2 — write its maximum value.**
f_max = µ_s N = **µ_s mg** ✓
**Step 3 — apply Newton's second law.**
ma_max = µ_s mg
**a_max = µ_s g** ✓
**Step 4 — substitute.**
a_max = 0·3 x 10
= **3·0 m s⁻²** ✓
**Why the mass cancels.** Both the required force and the available friction are
proportional to m ✓ so the limiting acceleration is the same for a 5 kg box and a
500 kg crate. The 50 kg is given only to see whether that is recognised.
**What happens beyond this acceleration.** Friction can no longer keep the box moving
with the train ✓ The box **slips backward** relative to the floor - which is what
happens to unsecured luggage when a train starts sharply.
**Which direction the friction acts.** **Forward**, in the direction of the train's
acceleration ✓ a counter-intuitive but essential point: friction here is the **driving**
force on the box, not a retarding one.
**The force involved at the limit.**
f = µmg = 0·3 x 50 x 10 = **150 N** ✓ and the box's acceleration is 150/50 = 3 m s⁻²,
matching the train's.
**Why static and not kinetic friction.** As long as the box does **not** slip, the
contact is static ✓ Static friction adjusts itself to whatever value is needed, up to
µ_sN; beyond that it gives way to the smaller kinetic value and the box slides.
**The same calculation elsewhere.** It fixes the maximum braking deceleration of a car,
the maximum speed round an unbanked bend, and the steepest slope a block will rest
on ✓ In each case the answer is µg or an angle whose tangent is µ.
**A sense of scale.** 3 m s⁻² is brisk for a train ✓ reaching 100 km/h in about 9
seconds - which is why metro trains with standing passengers accelerate more gently.
**Reading the distractors.** **5·0 m s⁻²** ✗ would need µ = 0·5. **1·5 m s⁻²** ✗ halves
the answer, and **15 m s⁻²** ✗ is five times too large - it would require µ = 1·5,
higher than most dry contacts ✓
∴ 3.0 ms⁻².

The fragments carry **equal and opposite momenta**, so the 8 kg piece also has
**20 N s**.
**Step 1 — conserve momentum.** The bomb was at rest, so the total momentum stays
zero ✓
p₈ = p₄ = **20 N s** in magnitude, oppositely directed.
**Step 2 — express the kinetic energy through momentum.**
KE = **p²/(2m)** ✓
**Step 3 — substitute for the 8 kg piece.**
KE = (20)²/(2 x 8)
= 400/16
= **25 J** ✓
**The other fragment, for comparison.**
KE₄ = 400/(2 x 4) = **50 J** ✓ twice as much, from the same momentum - because it is
half the mass.
**Why the lighter piece gets more energy.** With equal momentum, KE = p²/2m is
**inversely** proportional to the mass ✓ The light fragment must move faster, and
energy depends on the **square** of the speed.
**The speeds.**
4 kg piece: v = 20/4 = **5 m s⁻¹** ✓
8 kg piece: v = 20/8 = **2·5 m s⁻¹** ✓ half as fast, as the mass ratio demands.
**The total energy released.**
50 + 25 = **75 J** ✓ all of it supplied by the explosive. Kinetic energy is **created**
here, which is why only **momentum** may be conserved in an explosion.
**Why momentum and not energy is conserved.** Momentum conservation follows from
Newton's third law and requires no assumption about the forces ✓ Energy conservation
would hold only if no chemical energy were released - but releasing it is precisely
what an explosion does.
**The everyday analogue.** A rifle and its bullet ✓ equal and opposite momenta, but the
light bullet carries nearly all the energy while the heavy rifle merely recoils. The
same arithmetic, with a mass ratio of a thousand rather than two.
**A check on the directions.** The two pieces fly **exactly opposite** ✓ since a
two-body explosion from rest must be collinear - any transverse components would have
to cancel, and with only two fragments they can only do so by vanishing.
**Reading the distractors.** **50 J** ✗ is the **4 kg** piece's energy. **20 J** ✗ is
the momentum read as an energy, and **40 J** ✗ matches no step ✓
∴ 25 J.

The centre of mass lies **towards the heavier part** - deep in the sand, not in the
air.
**Step 1 — compare the two densities.** The box is divided diagonally: **air** above
and **sand** below ✓ Sand is some **1500 times** denser than air.
**Step 2 — see where the mass is.** Essentially **all** of it is in the sand ✓ The air's
contribution to the combined centre of mass is utterly negligible.
**Step 3 — locate the centre of mass.** It must lie at the centroid of the **sand**
region, with only an imperceptible shift towards the air ✓ Of the points marked, that
is **D**, which lies within the sand.
**Why the geometric centre is wrong.** The centre of mass is a **mass-weighted**
average, not a geometric one ✓
r̄_cm = **(m₁r̄₁ + m₂r̄₂)/(m₁ + m₂)** ✓
With m_sand ≫ m_air the second term dominates entirely.
**A numerical estimate.** Taking ρ_air = 1·2 and ρ_sand = 1600 kg m⁻³, the air
contributes a fraction
1·2/(1·2 + 1600) = **0·075%** ✓ so the centre of mass sits within a thousandth of the
sand's own centroid.
**Why the points in the air are impossible.** A and B lie in the **air** region ✓ The
centre of mass of a two-part system always lies **between** the two centroids, and here
it must be overwhelmingly near the sand's.
**Where the centre of mass of a uniform triangle lies.** At its **centroid**, one third
of the way from the base to the apex ✓ which for the sand's triangular region places it
well inside - consistent with D.
**Why the centre of mass need not be inside the material at all.** For a ring or a
horseshoe it lies in **empty space** ✓ Here it happens to fall within the sand, but
that is a feature of this particular geometry.
**Why the concept matters.** The whole system behaves, for translational purposes, as
though all its mass were concentrated at that point ✓ Thrown into the air, the box
would follow a parabola traced by exactly this point.
**The practical analogue.** Loading a ship or an aircraft ✓ The centre of mass must
stay within strict limits, and it is always dominated by the densest cargo.
**Reading the distractors.** **A** and **B** ✗ lie in the air. **C** ✗ lies near the
boundary ✓ Only D is properly within the mass.
∴ D.

The body with the **smallest** moment of inertia for its mass arrives **fastest** - the
sphere.
**Step 1 — write the speed at the bottom.** From energy conservation, with
I = kmR²:
mgh = ½mv²(1 + k)
**v = √[2gh/(1 + k)]** ✓
**Step 2 — list the k values.**
ring: k = **1** ✓
solid cylinder: k = **1/2** ✓
solid sphere: k = **2/5** ✓
**Step 3 — rank the speeds.** A larger k means a slower body:
**v_R < v_C < v_S** ✓
**Step 4 — compute the factors.**
ring: v = √(2gh/2) = **0·707√(2gh)** ✓
cylinder: √(2gh/1·5) = **0·816√(2gh)** ✓
sphere: √(2gh/1·4) = **0·845√(2gh)** ✓
**Why the mass and radius do not matter.** Both cancel from the energy equation ✓ Only
the **distribution** of mass, captured by k, decides the order. A marble and a cannon
ball of the same shape arrive together.
**Why the ring is slowest.** All its mass sits at the **maximum** distance from the
axis ✓ so it stores the largest share of the energy as rotation - **half** of it,
against the sphere's two sevenths.
**How the energy divides.**
ring: 50% translational, **50%** rotational ✓
cylinder: 67% / 33% ✓
sphere: **71%** / 29% ✓
**The accelerations.** a = g sin θ/(1 + k) ✓ so the sphere accelerates fastest and the
ring slowest, in the same order.
**A memorable demonstration.** Release a ring, a cylinder and a sphere together down a
ramp ✓ They finish in the order sphere, cylinder, ring - every time, regardless of
their sizes or masses. It is one of the most striking results in rotational mechanics.
**Why a sliding block would beat them all.** With no rotation, k = 0 and
v = **√(2gh)** ✓ The rolling bodies must spend part of their energy on spin, so none
can match a frictionless slide.
**Why friction does no work here.** At the contact point a rolling body is
**instantaneously at rest** ✓ so static friction, although essential for rolling,
dissipates nothing and energy is conserved.
**Reading the distractors.** **All equal** ✗ ignores the different k. **v_R > v_C >
v_S** ✗ reverses the order, and **v_R = v_C > v_S** ✗ wrongly equates two different
values of k ✓
∴ v_R < v_C < v_S.

Inside the Earth g rises **linearly**; outside it falls as **1/x²**.
**Step 1 — find g inside.** At a distance x < R, only the mass **within** that radius
attracts - the shell outside exerts no net force ✓ With uniform density,
M_enclosed ∝ x³, so
g = GM_enclosed/x² ∝ x³/x² = **x** ✓ a straight line through the origin.
**Step 2 — find g outside.** For x > R the whole mass acts as though concentrated at
the centre:
g = GM/x² ∝ **1/x²** ✓ a falling inverse-square curve.
**Step 3 — identify the graph.** A straight line rising from the origin to a **peak at
x = R**, then a smooth inverse-square decay ✓ That is the fourth figure.
**The value at the surface.** The two expressions must agree at x = R:
g = **GM/R² = 9·8 m s⁻²** ✓ the maximum, and the graph's peak.
**The two limits.**
at the **centre**, x = 0: g = **0** ✓ mass pulls equally in all directions
as x → ∞: g → **0** ✓ from the inverse square
So the curve rises from zero, peaks at the surface and decays to zero again.
**Why the shell theorem matters.** It is what makes the interior behaviour linear ✓ A
spherical shell exerts **no** gravitational force on anything inside it - a result
Newton proved, and the reason only the enclosed mass counts.
**The formulas, side by side.**
inside: g = **g_s(x/R)** ✓
outside: g = **g_s(R/x)²** ✓
**Which falls faster near the surface.** Going **up**, g ∝ 1/x², so a 1 km rise costs
about **0·31%** ✓ Going **down**, g ∝ x, so a 1 km descent costs only **0·16%** - half
as much. Gravity weakens twice as fast upward as downward.
**The real Earth, for honesty.** It is **not** uniform ✓ The dense iron core means g
actually **increases** slightly with depth down to the core-mantle boundary, peaking
near **10·7 m s⁻²** before falling to zero at the centre. The linear result assumes
uniform density.
**Reading the distractors.** Curves that **fall** inside ✗ contradict g ∝ x. Curves
that keep **rising** outside ✗ contradict the inverse square. A curve that **jumps** at
R ✗ would make g discontinuous, which it is not ✓
∴ the fourth graph.

Stretching a helical spring deforms the wire by **twisting**, so both longitudinal and
shear strains are present.
**Step 1 — look at the wire, not the spring.** Pulling the spring's free end does not
stretch the wire along its own length to any great extent ✓ It **unwinds** the helix
slightly, and the wire is principally **twisted**.
**Step 2 — identify the strains.** The dominant deformation is **shear** - the
torsional twisting of the wire ✓ accompanied by a smaller **longitudinal** extension as
the coils straighten.
**Step 3 — conclude.** The strain produced is **longitudinal and shear** ✓
**Why torsion dominates.** The wire runs almost **perpendicular** to the applied
force ✓ so the load acts at a lever arm equal to the coil radius, applying a **torque**
along the wire rather than a direct pull. That is why the spring's stiffness depends on
the **rigidity modulus** G, not on Young's modulus.
**The spring constant.**
k = **Gd⁴/(8nD³)** ✓
with d the wire diameter, D the coil diameter and n the number of turns. **G** - the
shear modulus - is what appears, confirming that twisting is the main deformation.
**Why a thin wire makes a soft spring.** k ∝ **d⁴** ✓ so halving the wire diameter makes
the spring **sixteen times** softer. Doubling the coil diameter makes it eight times
softer, since k ∝ 1/D³.
**Why a spring stores so much energy for its size.** The wire is stressed nearly
**uniformly** along its whole length ✓ Every part of it works, unlike a bent beam where
the material near the neutral axis does nothing.
**The two moduli distinguished.**
**Young's modulus Y**: resists **stretching** - a straight wire under tension ✓
**rigidity modulus G**: resists **shearing** - a twisted wire ✓
A straight wire pulled lengthwise shows pure longitudinal strain; a coiled one shows
mainly shear.
**Why the longitudinal part is not zero.** As the helix opens out, the wire does extend
slightly and the pitch angle changes ✓ so a small longitudinal strain accompanies the
dominant shear - which is why the answer names **both**.
**Reading the distractors.** **Volumetric** ✗ would need a change of volume, which
stretching a spring scarcely causes. **Shear** alone ✗ and **longitudinal** alone ✗ each
name only half the deformation ✓
∴ Longitudinal & Shear.

The **equation of continuity** makes the speed inversely proportional to the
**area** - and area goes as **d²**.
**Step 1 — state the principle.**
A_A v_A = A_B v_B ✓
so
**v ∝ 1/A** ✓
**Step 2 — compare the areas.** A ∝ d², and the diameters are 5 cm and 10 cm:
A_A : A_B = 5² : 10² = **1 : 4** ✓
**Step 3 — form the velocity ratio.**
v_A/v_B = A_B/A_A
= **4 : 1** ✓
**Why the diameter counts twice over.** Area goes as the **square** of the diameter ✓
so doubling the diameter quadruples the area and quarters the speed. Taking the ratio
as 2 : 1 - the diameter ratio - is the commonest error, and it is the third option.
**Why continuity must hold.** The fluid is **incompressible** and conserved ✓ Whatever
volume passes A each second must pass B each second, so a smaller opening forces a
higher speed.
**The flow rate, which is the same throughout.**
Q = Av ✓ constant along the pipe, in m³ s⁻¹.
**The pressure, by contrast.** By **Bernoulli's** principle, where the speed is higher
the pressure is **lower** ✓ so the narrow end A is at the **lower** pressure - the
basis of the venturi meter, the carburettor and the aspirator pump.
**A worked instance.** With Q = 0·01 m³ s⁻¹:
at A: A = π(0·025)² = 1·96 x 10⁻³ m², so v = **5·1 m s⁻¹** ✓
at B: A = 7·85 x 10⁻³ m², so v = **1·27 m s⁻¹** ✓
ratio **4 : 1** ✓
**The everyday demonstration.** Put a thumb over the end of a hose ✓ The same water per
second must escape through a quarter of the area, so it leaves four times as fast and
travels much further.
**The assumptions.** Steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow ✓ For a gas at high speed
the density changes and continuity must be written as ρAv = constant.
**Reading the distractors.** **1 : 4** ✗ inverts the ratio, giving the **narrow** end
the lower speed. **2 : 1** ✗ and **1 : 2** ✗ use the diameter ratio without squaring ✓
∴ 4 : 1.

Newton's law of cooling: the rate is proportional to the **excess temperature** above
the surroundings.
**Step 1 — handle the first cooling.** From 94 °C to 86 °C in 2 minutes:
drop = **8 °C**
mean temperature = **90 °C**, so the excess over 20 °C is **70 °C** ✓
8/2 = k(70), giving **k = 4/70 = 0·0571** ✓
**Step 2 — handle the second.** From 74 °C to 66 °C:
drop = **8 °C**
mean temperature = **70 °C**, excess **50 °C** ✓
**Step 3 — find the time.**
8/t = k(50) = 0·0571(50) = 2·857
**t = 8/2·857 = 2·8 minutes** ✓
**Why the second cooling is slower.** The pan is **cooler**, so the excess over the
room has fallen from 70 °C to 50 °C ✓ The driving temperature difference is smaller, so
the same 8 °C drop takes longer - 2·8 minutes against 2.
**The ratio, directly.**
t₂/t₁ = excess₁/excess₂ = 70/50 = **1·4** ✓
and 2 x 1·4 = **2·8 minutes** ✓ in one line, since the drops are equal.
**The approximation used.** For a small drop, the rate may be evaluated at the **mean**
temperature of the interval ✓ Here 8 °C against excesses of 70 and 50 - acceptable, and
standard in such problems.
**Why Newton's law holds only for small excesses.** It is the **linearisation** of
Stefan's T⁴ law ✓
T⁴ − T₀⁴ ≈ 4T₀³(T − T₀) for T close to T₀
For large differences, real cooling is faster than Newton predicts.
**The exponential form.**
T − T₀ = (T_i − T₀)e^(−kt) ✓
which gives the same answer exactly, with logarithms - but the mean-temperature method
is far quicker for small drops.
**How long to reach 40 °C.** Using the exponential form with k = 0·0571 min⁻¹:
20 = 74e^(−0·0571t) ... from 94 °C it would take about **36 minutes** ✓ and the
approach to room temperature is asymptotic - it never quite arrives.
**Where the law is used.** Estimating the time of death from body temperature, timing
the cooling of castings, and the standard calorimetry experiment ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **2 minutes** ✗ ignores the reduced excess. **2·5** ✗ and
**1·8 minutes** ✗ correspond to excess ratios of 1·25 and 0·9 ✓ Only 70/50 = 1·4 fits.
∴ 2.8 minutes.
